issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
The trauma that brought David to my office happened twenty-four years ago, during a deployment in a city that no longer appears on any map he cares to look at. He was a squad leader, twenty-five years old, when an improvised device detonated inside a market stall he was passing. The blast threw him forward into a pile of burlap sacks, and when he turned around, the man who had been walking beside him was no longer there in any recognizable form. David remembers the heat, the ringing, the way his hands moved to his weapon before his brain had caught up, but he does not remember the next several minutes. He knows he must have radioed for help, must have dragged someone to cover, but those moments exist only as a blank space that his mind refuses to fill. When he tries to tell the story now—to his wife, to the Veterans Affairs counselor he saw once and never returned to—the words stop coming. He loses the thread, the sequence, the logic of what happened, and he ends up staring at the floor with his hands pressed flat against his thighs, the terror of that afternoon flooding back as though no time had passed at all.

In the years since, David built a life that looked solid from the outside. He married a woman named Karen, raised two daughters, and was elected to the city council in a small Midwestern town where his primary job is to approve zoning variances and attend ribbon cuttings. But the world he walks through every day does not feel safe to him. It feels like a place where something terrible is always about to happen, and he cannot shake the conviction that his own body is part of the problem. His heart races at the grocery store for no reason. His hands tremble during committee meetings. He has come to believe that his body is an enemy that keeps signaling danger even when he knows, intellectually, that he is standing in a conference room full of people who are discussing stormwater drainage.

David has developed a quiet, elaborate system for managing this. He monitors his own thoughts constantly, scanning for signs that he is losing control, that he is about to snap or break down in public. He puts on loud music or leaves the television running in every room of the house, using the noise to drown out the internal static that threatens to pull him back into that market. The most difficult strategy, and the one that has caused the most trouble, is his avoidance of physical contact. David cannot bear to be touched. A hand on his shoulder from a colleague at city hall makes him flinch so violently that he has had to invent excuses—a pulled muscle, a sore back, a story about a car accident. At home, he has learned to angle his body away from Karen in the kitchen, to step back when she reaches for him, to lie rigid in bed and pretend to be asleep so that she will not roll toward him in the night. He knows she has noticed. He has seen the hurt flicker across her face, and he has not been able to explain why he cannot let her touch him without feeling like he is back in that market, waiting for the next explosion.

Sleep is almost impossible. He lies awake for hours, his body tensed for a sound that never comes, and when he does drift off he wakes in a startle, his arm already raised, his heart hammering. The startle response has become a constant companion. If someone touches him unexpectedly—a waitress brushing his elbow, a constituent reaching to shake his hand—he reacts with a visible alarm that he then has to laugh off, to explain away, to pretend was nothing. People tell him he is safe. Karen tells him. His doctor tells him. But David finds it impossible to believe. The words arrive in his ears and dissolve before they can mean anything.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in a council meeting three weeks ago. A colleague placed a hand on his back to guide him toward the podium, and David spun around so fast that he knocked a glass of water off the table. The room went quiet. Someone asked if he was okay. He said he was fine, but he saw the looks they exchanged, and he knew that something had shifted. He is afraid that he is losing the ability to function in the life he has built. He is afraid that his daughters are starting to notice. And he is afraid that if he stops monitoring, stops distracting, stops bracing himself against every touch, the thing he has been holding at bay for twenty-four years will finally break through and he will not survive it.
